<div class="subtitle-note">
Assistive robotics · Physical human-robot interaction · Wearable robotics ·
Multimodal learning · Nonlinear control
</div>

I build robotic systems that assist human mobility — powered exoskeletons,
actuated ankle-foot orthoses, and functional electrical stimulation (FES)
systems. The common thread is **human intent**: sensing it reliably from EMG
and IMU signals, inferring it in real time with machine learning, and turning
it into control actions that are precise enough to help and gentle enough to
trust. Much of this work has been validated in clinical trials.

## Research themes

::: {.entry}
<div class="entry-dates">Intent detection</div>
<div class="entry-body">
### Real-time human intent recognition
<p>LSTM- and attention-based models that classify gait modes and detect motion
intention from wearable sensors, reaching 98% accuracy while running fast
enough to drive an actuated orthosis in real time. Earlier work combined
Random Forests and deep learning with Kalman-filtered IMU features for robust
activity recognition.</p>
</div>
:::

::: {.entry}
<div class="entry-dates">Assistive control</div>
<div class="entry-body">
### Adaptive control for wearable robots
<p>Nonlinear control architectures for human-exoskeleton interaction:
impedance modulation for sit-to-stand assistance, fuzzy-adaptive and
funnel-based controllers for ankle-foot orthoses, and explicit model
predictive control for knee rehabilitation exoskeletons.</p>
</div>
:::

::: {.entry}
<div class="entry-dates">FES & clinics</div>
<div class="entry-body">
### Energy-efficient FES and clinical devices
<p>An EMG-driven adaptive FES strategy that cuts stimulation energy by 30%
while mitigating muscle fatigue in clinical trials, and a 7-IMU sensor-fusion
framework powering a portable device for lower-limb analysis and Parkinson's
disease assessment.</p>
</div>
:::

::: {.entry}
<div class="entry-dates">Motion AI</div>
<div class="entry-body">
### Physics-informed models of human motion
<p>Physics-informed AI models for motion intention inference, built on
motion-primitive representations of wearable IMU signals — work started at
KAIST with Dr. Jaegul Choo.</p>
</div>
:::
